Automation, AI, and the Transition to a Post-Labor Society
Nearly 70% of GDP in modern economies is driven by consumer spending. This creates a fundamental question for the future:
What happens if automation and AI eliminate large numbers of jobs, and consumers no longer have the income needed to participate in the economy?

One possible solution is not to resist automation, but to adapt civilization to it intelligently.
Tax the Robots: A Transitional Economic Model
Employees are expensive. From a business pective, robots and AI systems make economic sense because they can dramatically reduce costs while increasing efficiency and productivity.
However, there is a systemic contradiction: The same automation that increases corporate profits may simultaneously reduce the purchasing power of consumers.
A modern economy cannot function if productivity rises while consumer income collapses.
One possible solution is a robotic taxation system designed not to punish innovation, but to stabilize society during the transition toward a post-labor economy.
If a portion of the enormous productivity gains from automation were redistributed back into society, several things could happen simultaneously:
Companies would still benefit from massive efficiency gains.
Citizens could maintain purchasing power.

Another issue rarely discussed is whether modern labor systems are psychologically compatible with human beings.

The real challenge is not whether this transformation is coming.
The real challenge is whether humanity managems the transition wisely — or attempts to force industrial-age economic systems to operate in a world where intelligent machines can increasingly replace human labor.
